clue.text: Betrayed, in the end, as love letters may be

definitions.meaning: to be deceived by someone pretending to be on your side, cheated by an ally

definitions.text: in the end, as love letters may be
definitions.meaning: love letters often finish with two kisses written as XX, so their ending is marked twice with a cross

explanation.surface: A jilted lover reflects that, as the romance ends, the love letters prove to be a betrayal too.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: a letter signed off with XX has been crossed twice at its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for cheated by a supposed friend; the second sense is a punning literal reading of kisses as crosses.

clue.text: Decline victory in second half of high jump

indicators.note: the victory word is placed inside the trimmed jump word
only the latter four of the eight letters of the jump technique are kept

parts.note: the straddle is a style of high jump, rolling face-down over the bar
a victory is a win

explanation.surface: An athlete's form fades: a hoped-for victory slips away in the latter part of the high jump competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High jump' must first become a named technique, the straddle, a face-down roll over the bar; 'second half of' then keeps its last four letters, which take the victory word inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as verbs: to decline is to shrink or diminish gradually.

clue.text: Combination often going after European credit company

definitions.meaning: a joining together of parts, an alliance or merger

definitions.text: often going after European credit company
definitions.meaning: the word that commonly follows each of European, credit and company, as in the bloc, the savings co-operative and the workers' body

explanation.surface: A merger, frequently following a European credit firm, is described in financial-page terms.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a fill-in-the-blank: the same word completes three familiar phrases, each formed with European, credit or company placed before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a combination of parties or things joined together is an alliance or merger.

clue.text: Shoes for sale, brand-new

indicators.note: something brand-new is freshly made, so the letters of the two words are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A shop sign advertises footwear available to buy, never worn.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: slip-on casual leather footwear without laces goes by this name.

clue.text: Intruder chickens out, note, when disturbed

indicators.note: to be disturbed is to be thrown into disorder, so the letters of the three words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A trespasser frightens the hens, which flee, while a warning note is upset in the commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is only a link; the anagram is signalled by 'disturbed' and uses all of 'chickens out, note'.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the phrase names an unwelcome interloper, after the bird that lays its egg in other birds' nests.

clue.text: Yellowish old church on River Ely left deserted

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river

indicators.note: to be deserted is to be abandoned, so the left letter quits the town name

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England

explanation.surface: An abandoned, faded old church stands beside the river at Ely, a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deserted' takes the 'left' letter out of the city name, leaving EY; 'on' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the adjective describes a colour like the earthy yellow-brown pigment used by painters.

clue.text: Rep extremely shady about drinks with boy

indicators.note: the outer letters go around the drinks and the boy, enclosing them
only the extreme letters of the word shady are taken

parts.note: ales are beers, drinks in a pub
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A dodgy sales representative is seen round the pub buying drinks with a young lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes only the two end letters of shady, and 'about' puts them around the drinks and the boy; 'with' only joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a female shop assistant or commercial representative is one kind of sales rep.

clue.text: Reveal identity of chap about to break into memory device

indicators.note: the reversed name forces its way inside the storage word

parts.note: a disk is a computer storage device

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Sam is a typical man's name, a chap

explanation.surface: Detectives learn who a man is after he breaks into a computer storage unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the chap's name round to MAS, and 'to break into' sends that inside the storage word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to take off a disguise or mask, so to expose who someone really is.

clue.text: Top-level racing judge, one in a state

parts.note: Formula One, F1, is the top level of motor racing, with the figure 1 written as the letter I
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A senior motor-racing steward, it seems, is in a terrible state.
explanation.walkthrough: F1 is read with its digit as a letter I; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Pacific island republic is a sovereign nation, a country in its own right.

clue.text: In which local drunk without house is ultimately grim

definitions.text: In which local drunk without house is ultimately grim

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the jumbled letters wrap the house abbreviation
drunk suggests reeling about, so the letters of local and is are mixed up
ultimately points to the final letter of grim

explanation.surface: A grim picture of addiction: the pub regular, drunk and homeless, comes to a bad end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles two clue words into ALCOLIS; 'without', in its old sense of outside, wraps that round the house abbreviation; 'ultimately' adds the last letter of grim.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the dependency on drink that leaves a pub regular homeless and in a sorry state.

clue.text: European port in which everything's sparse?

definitions.meaning: a harbour city in Europe, here in Denmark on the island of Funen
split as O and DENSE, it suggests a place where nothing (zero) is dense, so all is thinly spread

explanation.surface: A puzzling travel note about a European harbour town that feels thinly populated.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags whimsy: O for nothing, then DENSE, reads as 'nothing is dense', hence everything is sparse.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Danish city, birthplace of Hans Christian Andersen, is a port on the island of Funen.

clue.text: Deliveries by a river remain too long

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, so deliveries gives overs
the Tay is Scotland's longest river

explanation.surface: Parcels left beside a river sit there longer than they should.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls (deliveries); 'by a' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to outstay one's welcome is to linger beyond the allotted time.

clue.text: Genuine article is switched

indicators.note: switched means swapped around, so the letters of article and is are rearranged

explanation.surface: A buyer complains that a supposedly authentic item has been swapped for a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: true to life, lifelike and authentic rather than fake or fanciful.

clue.text: Meat brands in a plant

parts.note: lamb is a meat
to brand is to burn a mark, to sear

explanation.surface: A puzzle about meat labels appearing in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brands' is a verb, not trade names; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the woolly-leaved garden perennial Stachys byzantina is known by this name for its soft foliage.

clue.text: Note minute chest

parts.note: an ark is a chest or coffer, as in the Ark of the Covenant

explanation.surface: A reminder to write down a tiny chest.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as verbs: to note something is to take notice of it or observe it.

clue.text: Knock the majority of boring documents

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: bumph is British slang for tedious paperwork

explanation.surface: An office worker criticises most of the dull paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: BUMPH (also spelt bumf) is British slang for dreary official paperwork; dropping its last letter leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a knock is a blow or a bang, like one taken against a door frame.

clue.text: Viewer runs into tanker

indicators.note: the runs abbreviation goes inside the tanker word

parts.note: a bowser is a tanker carrying fuel or water
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A spectator crashes into a fuel lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: A bowser is a British term for a tanker truck supplying fuel or water.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone casually looking through goods or web pages is a viewer, as is the software that displays websites.

clue.text: Remaining around English duke, independently providing support

indicators.note: the two letters are placed separately, each at its own spot in the remaining word
the remaining word goes around the inserted letters

parts.note: remaining means staying

explanation.surface: An English duke stays on, acting on his own, to prop someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'independently' tells you E and D go into STAYING separately rather than as ED together: ST-E-A-D-YING.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: steadying something keeps it firm, so to give it support.

clue.text: Grounds for university to be exposed over support for Pistorius, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first part sits above the second
exposing strips away the outer covering, so the first and last letters are removed

parts.note: a campus is the grounds of a university
a tee is the peg supporting a golf ball

explanation.surface: Students protest that university grounds are being laid bare to build facilities for the Paralympian.
explanation.walkthrough: Exposing CAMPUS removes its ends to leave AMPU. Oscar Pistorius was a South African sprinter who ran on prosthetic blades.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the athlete had both lower legs removed in infancy, making him a person who has lost limbs.

clue.text: Surely bound to change

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters in the two preceding words

explanation.surface: Someone insists that something is certain to alter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to' looks like part of the surface meaning 'certain to', but it is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both words express certainty, used as sentence adverbs meaning certainly.

clue.text: Preachers appeal to chase flesh

indicators.note: to chase is to follow behind, so the appeal word comes after the flesh word

parts.note: pulp is the soft flesh of fruit
it is slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Clergy urge the faithful to pursue the pleasures of the flesh, an ironic sermon.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal is old slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Metonymy: the raised stand in church stands for the clergy collectively, as 'the press' stands for journalists.

clue.text: Again touring Uist in a storm in which you'd get wet

indicators.note: the again word travels around the shuffled island name

parts.note: more means again, as in once more

indicators.note: a storm tosses things about, so the island's letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A visitor travels round the Hebridean island of Uist once more in a storm and gets soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: Uist is an island group in Scotland's Outer Hebrides; 'in a storm' scrambles it to ISTU, and 'touring' puts the word for again around that.
explanation.definitionFit: Being surrounded by dampness or water vapour leaves you damp, so the wetness itself is meant.

clue.text: One must leave platforms outside a grand temple

indicators.note: the shortened platforms word sits around the other two pieces
the letter for one has to depart from the platforms word

parts.note: podia are raised platforms, plural of podium
I is the Roman numeral one
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: One person has to step off the stages set up outside an impressive temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must leave' removes I from PODIA to give PODA, which goes 'outside' A and G.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the tiered tower found in East Asian Buddhist sites is a type of temple.

clue.text: Female game involved catching male

indicators.note: the jumbled game letters catch the male abbreviation inside them
involved means intricate or tangled, so the game letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A woman joins a game and ends up catching a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges GAME as GEMA, which takes M inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the girl's name is one that a female might have.

clue.text: Face wound regularly pumped in hospital department

indicators.note: the scar and selected letters go inside the department abbreviation

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital
a scar is the mark of a wound

indicators.note: regularly picks every other letter of pumped

explanation.surface: A patient with a facial wound has been pumped full of fluids in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes alternate letters of pumped, giving PME; 'in' puts the wound and those letters inside the ear, nose and throat department.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography: a steep slope or cliff, the steep face of a ridge, is called this.

clue.text: Hammer gold medal, having lost heart when touring

indicators.note: the remains of the medal word travel around the gold symbol
the medal word loses all its inner letters, leaving its outer pair

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A disheartened athlete on tour smashes their gold medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost heart' leaves M and L from medal, which go round AU; 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as verbs: to maul an opponent is to batter or thrash them, as a sports team might.

clue.text: Wild sabre-tooth tiger, mostly not good, reacted when provoked

indicators.note: wild means uncontrolled and disordered, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement
not tells us the good abbreviation is taken away
most of the word tiger is used, its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: A wild prehistoric cat, mostly bad-tempered, lashed out when goaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts TIGER to TIGE and 'not good' drops the G, leaving TIE; 'Wild' then shuffles SABRETOOTH plus TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: like a fish taking the hook, the phrase means responded angrily to a taunt.
